takeaway: Eden adds hints only where most page faults originate, combining user-space far-memory policies with hardware fallback faults to reduce porting effort and paging overhead.
background: Far memory lets a server borrow remote DRAM, but accessing a nonresident page is much slower than local memory. Page-based systems are transparent yet fault-heavy; object-integrated systems expose better policies but require pervasive software guards.
villain: Existing designs force applications to choose between expensive kernel-mediated page faults and invasive object-level ports whose guards also tax local accesses.
approach: A profiling tool finds the small set of source locations that cause most faults, where developers add hint_fault annotations carrying an address and optional read-ahead or eviction guidance. On a hint, Eden's Shenango-based runtime checks page metadata, fetches missing pages over RDMA, and runs another user-level thread during the fetch; unhinted hardware faults fall back to a control core through userfaultfd. Because Linux retains page-table control, Eden batches noncontiguous write-protect and unmap operations through new vectorized syscalls.
impact: The authors argue that sparse hints provide much of an object-integrated far-memory system's policy flexibility while retaining page-based compatibility and requiring substantially fewer application changes.

evaluation.overview: The authors measure developer effort, application performance across local-memory fractions, and component microbenchmarks on four C/C++ workloads.
evaluation.implemented: A Shenango-based C/C++ runtime, RDMA client and memory server, fault-location profiler, LD_PRELOAD allocator interposition, and Linux kernel patch for vectorized syscalls.
evaluation.setting: Eden and Fastswap run on three Linux servers with 100-Gbps ConnectX-5 NICs; AIFM and TrackFM use their CloudLab artifact setups, so cross-system results are normalized to each system's fully local native baseline.
baselines: Each system's fully local native application configuration

results.text: The authors report that, across DataFrame, the synthetic Web service, Memcached, and parallel sort, each application's maximum gain over Fastswap was between 19.4% and 178%, depending on workload and local-memory setting.
The authors report that, for DataFrame, 11 single-line hints covered 97.3% of page faults; the AIFM port changed 1,192 lines, or 108× more changes.
results.locator: PDF pp. 3 and 9–10 (paper pp. 1068 and 1074–1075); §1, §5.2, Table 1, and Listing 1

limitations: The prototype assumes RDMA far memory, profiled source annotations, a Shenango-style user-level scheduler, and a patched Linux kernel for vectorized calls. Page granularity amplifies cache and network I/O for small objects with poor locality, while unhinted misses take an especially costly userfaultfd path.
phd_group_signal: This work reflects an operating-systems style that starts from workload profiling, chooses a hybrid abstraction, modifies the runtime and kernel boundary, and evaluates both programmer effort and end-to-end performance.

claims.text: Eden places software guards at profiled high-fault code locations and uses hardware page faults elsewhere; hints trigger user-space RDMA fetches, scheduling during misses, and application-guided read-ahead or reclamation.

The evaluated prototype builds on Shenango, uses RDMA for far-memory transfers, relies on Linux userfaultfd for page-table operations and fallback faults, and adds vectorized kernel interfaces for write protection and unmapping.

The paper reports that page-sized management loses efficiency on small objects with poor spatial locality and that Eden's miss path, especially an unhinted kernel trap, is slower than pure application-integrated handling.
claims.locator: PDF pp. 11 and 13 (paper pp. 1076 and 1078); §5.3.2 and §7
